P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, but under exchange control. The Exchange and Foreign Trade Code (Law 76-18, art. 20) requires every resident individual to repatriate all foreign currency earned from services rendered abroad, under BCT conditions and deadlines. Freelancers, consultants and other providers serving non-residents outside Tunisia can open a PPR account in foreign currency or convertible dinars and credit their service fees to it (BCT circular 2017-04), so the proceeds need not all be converted. A PPR holder may not keep bank balances abroad. Locally, Konnect (a BCT-certified payment facilitator) lets freelancers take international Visa/Mastercard payments, settled in Tunisia.

No BCT circular after 2017 on freelancer proceeds was found. A pending bill (36/2026) and a new exchange code bill (115/2025) are not law.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes, two ways. (1) The PPR account (BCT circular 2017-04): one per person, for listed categories that include providers of services to non-residents abroad. It is credited with their foreign service fees and can be debited for conversion, documented personal payments abroad, and so on. (2) Since 1 January 2026, Finance Law 2026 (Law 2025-17, art. 98) lets resident individuals of Tunisian nationality open foreign-currency accounts with licensed intermediaries without prior BCT approval. These accounts can only be funded from another foreign-currency or convertible-dinar account, from interest, or from the annual tourist allowance. They can be debited for payments abroad, travel currency or another FX account, and can never be overdrawn.

P3_local_gateways.question: Which local payment gateways can an individual or sole trader use to accept online payments?
P3_local_gateways.answer: Global platform availability for Tunisia (automated collector snapshots, Oct 2026). Available: Paddle (not on its exclusion list; software sellers only, each seller reviewed); Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts); Polar (payouts); Whop (payouts); Dodo Payments (sellers); Google Play (developer registration); YouTube Partner Program. Not listed: Stripe (merchant sign-up); Etsy seller payments.

P3_local_gateways.notes: Konnect, a BCT-certified payment facilitator, onboards freelancers as well as companies online with identification documents. It offers payment links, CMS plugins and an API, accepts Tunisian cards, e-dinar and international Visa/Mastercard, and pays out to the merchant's Tunisian bank account. Konnect's site renders client-side; read in the built-in browser and saved as a text excerpt. Which identity or registration documents Konnect requires (CIN only, or tax ID/RNE) is not stated. Other local gateways (ClicToPay/SMT, Flouci) not researched.

P4_paypal.question: Can residents receive money via PayPal?
P4_paypal.answer: No. Tunisia is a listed PayPal market but is classed as 'send only': residents can pay but cannot normally receive income for their work. Tunisia is also absent from the Payouts list. An August 2026 private member's bill (36/2026) would open PayPal-type platforms to freelancers, with a 15% levy on withdrawals, a USD 5,000 monthly cap and automatic conversion to dinars. It is not law.

P5_payoneer_wise.question: Payoneer / Wise availability for residents
P5_payoneer_wise.answer: Wise: Tunisia is NOT on Wise's list of countries whose residents can hold money. Payoneer: no reliable 2026 source confirming availability for Tunisian residents was found. Whatever the channel, residents must repatriate foreign service earnings (Exchange Code art. 20), and PPR-account holders may not hold bank balances abroad, so foreign wallet balances are not a lawful place to keep earnings.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Simplest: the auto-entrepreneur regime (Decree-Law 2020-33). It is open to Tunisian nationals working individually in industry, agriculture, commerce, services, crafts or trades with annual turnover up to TND 75,000. Registration is online in the Registre national de l'auto-entrepreneur. Eligible activities are fixed by government decree, and whether a given digital service is listed was not verified. People who had already filed a tax 'déclaration d'existence' are excluded. Otherwise an individual files a déclaration d'existence with the tax office to get a tax ID. Registration in the Registre National des Entreprises (Law 2018-52) is mandatory for natural persons who are traders or carry on any other professional activity.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: The identifiant fiscal (matricule fiscal). File a déclaration d'existence on the administration's form at the competent tax control office (bureau de contrôle des impôts); premises may be visited, and the office head grants the ID 'immediately'. Natural persons attach a copy of their national ID card (CIN). The tax ID also serves as the unique identifier in the business register (RNE).

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Residents (principal home in Tunisia, or 183+ days a calendar year) pay personal income tax on worldwide income, except foreign income already taxed abroad. From 1 January 2025 the scale is 0% to TND 5,000, then rising bands of 15% up to 40% (upper band limits not captured). Auto-entrepreneurs instead pay a single contribution covering income tax, VAT and social security. The income-tax part is TND 200 a year (communal zones as at 2015) or TND 100 (other zones), plus the social contribution of the first bracket of the self-employed scheme. Nothing is due in the year of registration.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Standard VAT is 19% (VAT Code art. 7). Professional fees (consultants, experts, etc.) have been at 19% since 2023. A service is taxable in Tunisia only when it is used or exploited in Tunisia (art. 3), so services used by clients abroad are outside Tunisian VAT. Voluntary registration is possible for export-destined operations. No general turnover threshold for service providers was found. For auto-entrepreneurs the single contribution replaces VAT.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: Organic Law 2004-63: every processing of personal data requires a prior declaration to the INPDP (art. 7). Sensitive data needs authorisation, and cross-border transfers are restricted. Processing without the declaration is punishable by one year's imprisonment and a TND 5,000 fine (art. 90). A replacement organic law (draft 095/2025) is pending.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Law 2000-83 on electronic exchanges and commerce: the consumer may withdraw within 10 working days, counted from receipt for goods or from contract conclusion for services (art. 30), subject to the pre-contract information duties of art. 25. Exceptions (art. 32) include a service delivered before the period ends at the consumer's request, and personalised or perishable goods.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: (1) The auto-entrepreneur single contribution (L3), which replaces income tax, VAT and social security up to TND 75,000 turnover, with nothing due in the first year if the National Employment Fund covers social contributions. (2) The PPR foreign-currency account for service exporters, and resident FX accounts since 2026 (P2). (3) Services used abroad are outside Tunisian VAT (L4). Pending, not law: freelance bill 36/2026 (platform access with a 15% levy) and new exchange code bill 115/2025.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving); Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (6) Local official channel: Providers of services to non-residents can open a PPR foreign-currency account. Repatriation of foreign earnings is mandatory (Exchange Code art. 20) (P1/P2). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
